Asymptotics and periodic dynamics in a negative chemotaxis system with cell lethality

Journal: Nonlinear Analysis
Federico Herrero-Hervás Email: fedher01@ucm.es Corresponding author: Corresponding author Affiliation: Instituto de Matemática Interdisciplinar, Departamento de Análisis Matemático y Matemática Aplicada, Universidad Complutense de Madrid, Madrid, 28040, Spain Affiliation: Universität Paderborn, Paderborn, 33098, Germany Affiliation: Departamento de Matemática Aplicada, ICAI, Universidad Pontificia de Comillas, Madrid, 28015, Spain    Mihaela Negreanu Affiliation: Instituto de Matemática Interdisciplinar, Departamento de Análisis Matemático y Matemática Aplicada, Universidad Complutense de Madrid, Madrid, 28040, Spain
Abstract

This work studies the following system of parabolic partial differential equations

{∂u∂t=DΔu+χ∇⋅(u∇v)+ru(1−u)−uv,x∈Ω,t>0,∂v∂t=Δv+au−v+f(x,t),x∈Ω,t>0,\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}=D\Delta u+\chi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v)+ru(1-u)-uv,\quad&x\in\Omega,\penalty\ t>0,\\ \\ \displaystyle\frac{\partial v}{\partial t}=\Delta v+au-v+f(x,t),\quad&x\in\Omega,\penalty\ t>0,\end{cases}

modeling the negative chemotaxis interactions between a biological species and a lethal chemical substance that is supplied according to the known function f⁡(x,t)f(x,t).

It is shown that if ff converges to a spatially homogeneous function f~\tilde{f} in a certain sense, then the solution (u,v)(u,v) satisfies

‖u−u~‖L2​(Ω)+‖v−v~‖L2​(Ω)→0as ​t→∞,||u-\tilde{u}||_{L^{2}(\Omega)}+||v-\tilde{v}||_{L^{2}(\Omega)}\to 0\quad\text{as }t\to\infty,

where (u~,v~)(\tilde{u},\tilde{v}) is the solution to the associated ODE system

{d​u~d​t=ru~(1−u~)−u~v~,t>0,d​v~d​t=au~−v~+f~,t>0.\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{d\tilde{u}}{dt\penalty\ }=r\tilde{u}(1-\tilde{u})-\tilde{u}\tilde{v},\quad&t>0,\\ \\ \displaystyle\frac{d\tilde{v}}{dt\penalty\ }=a\tilde{u}-\tilde{v}+\tilde{f},\quad&t>0.\end{cases}

Some final remarks are given for the case in which f~\tilde{f} is a time periodic function, and under which hypotheses do (u~,v~)(\tilde{u},\tilde{v}) inherit this periodicity.

Keywords:
chemotaxis; periodicity; asymptotics; convergence; cross-diffusion

1 Introduction

This work is centered around the asymptotic behavior of the solution to the following system of two coupled nonlinear parabolic partial differential equations

{∂u∂t=DΔu+χ∇⋅(u∇v)+ru(1−u)−uv,x∈Ω,t>0,∂v∂t=Δv+au−v+f(x,t),x∈Ω,t>0,\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}=D\Delta u+\chi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v)+ru(1-u)-uv,\quad&x\in\Omega,\penalty\ t>0,\\ \\ \displaystyle\frac{\partial v}{\partial t}=\Delta v+au-v+f(x,t),\quad&x\in\Omega,\penalty\ t>0,\end{cases} (1)

subject to nonnegative initial values and Neumann homogeneous boundary conditions

{u(x,0)=u0(x)≥0,v(x,0)=v0(x)≥0,x∈Ω,∂u∂ν=∂v∂ν=0,x∈∂Ω,t>0,\begin{cases}u(x,0)=u_{0}(x)\geq 0,\quad v(x,0)=v_{0}(x)\geq 0,&x\in\Omega,\\ \\ \displaystyle\frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}=\frac{\partial v}{\partial\nu}=0,&x\in\partial\Omega,\penalty\ t>0,\end{cases} (2)

posed over a bounded and convex domain Ω⊂ℝn\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} with smooth boundary, with parameters D,χ,r>0,a≥0D,\penalty\ \chi,\penalty\ r>0,\penalty\ a\geq 0 and a nonnegative known source function f≥0f\geq 0.

System (1) has recently been proposed in [5] as a model for the interaction between a bacterial population and a lethal chemical agent, such as a toxin or an antibiotic. In the model, u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) denotes the bacterial density and v⁡(x,t)v(x,t) the concentration of the chemical at position x∈Ωx\in\Omega and time t>0t>0, accounting for the following mechanisms:

  1. 1.

    Cell motility and chemical diffusion, incorporated by the Laplacian terms Δ​u\Delta u and Δ​v\Delta v.

  2. 2.

    Negative chemotaxis, this is, bacterial repulsion from regions of high chemical concentration, described by χ∇⋅(u∇v)\chi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v).

  3. 3.

    Logistic bacterial growth and chemical lethality, modeled respectively by the terms r​u​(1−u)ru(1-u) and −u​v-uv.

  4. 4.

    Self-production and degradation of the chemical, captured by a​u−vau-v.

  5. 5.

    An external supply of the substance, represented by the source function ff.

These interactions considered for the model are common in microbiological systems where organisms react to toxins, antibiotics, or self-produced metabolic byproducts. This is the case for instance for E. coli bacteria and H2​O2H_{2}O_{2}. It is known that E. coli cells naturally produce H2​O2H_{2}O_{2} molecules [17, 16], which act as a lethal chemorepellent [3, 21, 8], leading to bacterial migration towards regions of lower concentrations in order to survive.

Although for most bacteria such as E. coli, the self production of a chemo-repellent is in general not a means of self regulation or signaling —but instead a consequence of their metabolism [9]—, its combination with the negative chemotaxis and the intrinsic dynamics of self-production, degradation, logistic growth and lethality creates an intricate feedback mechanism between bacterial motion and the interactions with the chemical, whose asymptotics are analyzed in this work.

We note as well that by allowing a=0a=0, the model also accounts for the interactions with an exogenous antibiotic, this is, when the chemical is not produced by the bacteria themselves.

From a mathematical point of view, the first models for chemotaxis were introduced by Keller and Segel [10, 11], considering the nonlinear term ∇⋅(u∇v)\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v). Over the years, the Keller-Segel model has been extensively studied, showing the rich behavior of its solutions, ranging from aggregation phenomena to finite-time blow-up (see for instance the surveys by Horstmann [7] or Hillen and Painter [6]).

In terms of global existence, it is well known that adding a logistic growth term to the model, resulting in a system of the form

{∂u∂t=D1Δu−χ∇⋅(u∇v)+ru−μu2,x∈Ω,t>0,τ​∂v∂t=D2​Δ​v+u−α​v,x∈Ω,t>0,\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}=D_{1}\Delta u-\chi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v)+ru-\mu u^{2},\quad&x\in\Omega,\penalty\ t>0,\\ \\ \displaystyle\tau\frac{\partial v}{\partial t}=D_{2}\Delta v+u-\alpha v,&x\in\Omega,\penalty\ t>0,\end{cases} (3)

under Neumann homogeneous boundary conditions and nonnegative initial values, can suppress the finite-time blow-up of solutions that certain solutions to the minimal Keller-Segel system experiment.

In particular, in Tello and Winkler [19], the parabolic-elliptic case (corresponding to τ=0\tau=0) is analyzed for positive chemotaxis (i.e. attractant signaling, with χ>0\chi>0). The authors prove that system (3) admits a unique solution that remains globally bounded for any parameter set, if the problem is posed over a bounded domain in dimension n≤2n\leq 2. Moreover, in the higher dimensional case, global boundedness still holds provided that the damping effect of the logistic term is sufficiently strong, specifically when μ>n−22​χ\mu>\displaystyle\frac{n-2}{2}\chi, so that the quadratic death term −μ​u2-\mu u^{2} dominates the aggregation induced by chemotaxis.

For the fully parabolic version (with τ>0\tau>0), system (3) was studied by Winkler in [22] for a general χ∈ℝ\chi\in\mathbb{R}, thus accounting for positive and negative chemotaxis, obtaining global boundedness of solutions in arbitrary dimensions for convex domains if μ\mu is large enough. For the positive chemotaxis case there exists M>0M>0 such that if μχ>M\displaystyle\frac{\mu}{\chi}>M, the unique non-trivial spatially homogeneous steady state of the system becomes globally asymptotically stable, and any solution (u,v)(u,v) converges to it, as proven in [23].

Our system (1) mainly differs from (3) not only in considering the negative chemotaxis scenario, but also in the asymmetrical death term −u​v-uv, —which does not have a counterpart on the vv equation, as cell death does not result in an increase of the chemical concentration—, and in the external supply ff, which greatly affects the dynamics of the system.

Several other works have addressed similar competitive terms, mainly in the form of Lotka-Volterra interactions between two species that are attracted by the same chemical. The elliptic case for the equation of the chemical was studied in [20] in a weakly competitive scenario, obtaining as well the convergence of solutions to the non-trivial spatially homogeneous steady state, under appropriate parameter restrictions. The parabolic case is considered as well in [2, 12, 24] with similar results for the asymptotic behavior of solutions.

A system closely related to ours is given by

{∂u∂t=Δu−χ∇(u∇v)+μu(1+f(x,t)−u),x∈Ω,t>0,τ​∂v∂t=Δ​v+u−v,x∈Ω,t>0,\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}=\Delta u-\chi\nabla(u\nabla v)+\mu u(1+f(x,t)-u),\quad&x\in\Omega,\penalty\ t>0,\\ \\ \displaystyle\tau\frac{\partial v}{\partial t}=\Delta v+u-v,&x\in\Omega,\penalty\ t>0,\end{cases} (4)

where the logistic term satisfies 1+f⁡(x,t)>01+f(x,t)>0, which can be interpreted as a spatio-temporal dependent carrying capacity for the biological species. In particular, the system is analyzed by Negreanu, Tello and Vargas in [14], with the assumption that f⁡(x,t)f(x,t) converges to a spatially homogeneous and time periodic function f~\tilde{f}, modeling seasonal fluctuations in the maximum population load that the environment can support. A generalization of system (4) with two species in competitive interaction and periodic logistic dynamics was introduced and studied in [15]

In particular, for system (4) in [14], under the assumptions that

f∈L∞​(Ω×(0,∞)),∫0∞∫Ω|∇f|2​dx​dt<∞,∫0∞‖f−f~‖L1​(Ω)​dt<∞,\begin{split}f\in L^{\infty}\big(\Omega\times(0,\infty)\big),\\ \\ \int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{\Omega}|\nabla f|^{2}dx\hskip 2.84544ptdt<\infty,\\ \\ \int_{0}^{\infty}||f-\tilde{f}||_{L^{1}(\Omega)}\hskip 2.84544ptdt<\infty,\end{split} (5)

as well as

μ>χ216​max​{∫Ωu0​𝑑x,1μ​(1+‖f‖L∞​(Ω×(0,∞)))},\mu>\frac{\chi^{2}}{16}\max\left\{\int_{\Omega}u_{0}\hskip 2.84544ptdx,\penalty\ \frac{1}{\mu}\left(1+||f||_{L^{\infty}(\Omega\times(0,\infty))}\right)\right\}, (6)

it is proven that any solution (u,v)(u,v) to (4) verifies

‖u−u~‖L2​(Ω)+‖v−v~‖L2​(Ω)→0,as ​t→∞,||u-\tilde{u}||_{L^{2}(\Omega)}+||v-\tilde{v}||_{L^{2}(\Omega)}\to 0,\quad\text{as }t\to\infty,

where (u~,v~)(\tilde{u},\tilde{v}) is the solution to the ODE system associated to system (4), this is

{d​u~d​t=μu~(1+f~(t)−u~),t>0,τ​d​v~d​t=u~−v~,t>0,\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{d\tilde{u}}{dt\penalty\ }=\mu\tilde{u}\big(1+\tilde{f}(t)-\tilde{u}\big),\quad&t>0,\\ \\ \displaystyle\tau\frac{d\tilde{v}}{dt\penalty\ }=\tilde{u}-\tilde{v},&t>0,\end{cases} (7)

with initial values

u~​(0)=∫Ωu0​(x)​𝑑x,v~​(0)=∫Ωv0​(x)​𝑑x.\tilde{u}(0)=\int_{\Omega}u_{0}(x)\hskip 2.84544ptdx,\quad\tilde{v}(0)=\int_{\Omega}v_{0}(x)\hskip 2.84544ptdx.

Main results and structure of the work

We recall our system, given by

{∂u∂t=DΔu+χ∇⋅(u∇v)+ru(1−u)−uv,x∈Ω,t>0,∂v∂t=Δv+au−v+f(x,t),x∈Ω,t>0,\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}=D\Delta u+\chi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v)+ru(1-u)-uv,\quad&x\in\Omega,\penalty\ t>0,\\ \\ \displaystyle\frac{\partial v}{\partial t}=\Delta v+au-v+f(x,t),\quad&x\in\Omega,\penalty\ t>0,\end{cases}

under Neumann homogeneous boundary conditions and nonnegative initial values. Our aim is to develop a similar analysis as done for system (4), considering that f⁡(x,t)f(x,t) converges in time (in a certain sense specified below) to a spatially homogeneous function f~​(t)\tilde{f}(t).

In this way, the main result of the work is Theorem 4.1, that ensures that if certain parameter conditions are met, any solution (u,v)(u,v) converges in L2​(Ω)L^{2}(\Omega) to (u~,v~)(\tilde{u},\tilde{v}), the corresponding solution to the ODE system associated to our system (1), given by

{d​u~d​t=ru~(1−u~)−u~v~,t>0,d​v~d​t=au~−v~+f~,t>0,\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{d\tilde{u}}{dt\penalty\ }=r\tilde{u}(1-\tilde{u})-\tilde{u}\tilde{v},\quad&t>0,\\ \\ \displaystyle\frac{d\tilde{v}}{dt\penalty\ }=a\tilde{u}-\tilde{v}+\tilde{f},\quad&t>0,\end{cases} (8)

with initial values

u~​(0)=∫Ωu0​(x)​𝑑x,v~​(0)=∫Ωv0​(x)​𝑑x.\tilde{u}(0)=\int_{\Omega}u_{0}(x)\penalty\ dx,\quad\tilde{v}(0)=\int_{\Omega}v_{0}(x)\penalty\ dx. (9)

This extends the existing information about solutions to system (1), which, to the best of our knowledge, only includes the qualitative analysis performed in [5] for constant choices of ff, as well as periodicity properties for the associated ODE system (8) in the case a=0a=0 and a time-periodic f~​(t)\tilde{f}(t). In particular, [5] proves that the balance between the logistic growth rate rr and the external supply of the chemical ff governs the linearized dynamics of the system.

More specifically, for a constant source, f⁡(x,t)≡f>0f(x,t)\equiv f>0, if f>rf>r, it is proven that the only nonnegative spatially homogeneous steady state (0,f)(0,f) is locally asymptotically stable, while if f<rf<r, there exists a secondary nonnegative equilibrium (u∗,v∗):=(r−fr+a,r⁡(f+a)r+a)(u_{*},v_{*})\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\left(\displaystyle\frac{r-f}{r+a},\frac{r(f+a)}{r+a}\right). In this case, (0,f)(0,f) is unstable, while (u∗,v∗)(u_{*},v_{*}) is locally asymptotically stable. The local dynamics were at times preserved globally, while certain parameter gave rise to aggregation phenomena in the form of spike patterns.

For the case in which a=0a=0 and f~​(t)\tilde{f}(t) is a time-periodic function of period T>0T>0, it is shown that if r>f~¯:=1T​∫0Tf~​(t)​𝑑tr>\bar{\tilde{f}}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\displaystyle\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}\tilde{f}(t)\hskip 2.84544ptdt, then system (8) admits a periodic solution of period TT, thus inheriting the periodicity of the source f~\tilde{f}. The convergence of solutions (u,v)(u,v) to (u~,v~)(\tilde{u},\tilde{v}) was only tested numerically with positive results.

In this way, the present work provides an analytical proof of the convergence of solutions to the full PDE system (1) to its associated ODE system (8), that holds as well for the more interesting case a>0a>0, when the second equation is not decoupled.

In particular, for the proof it is assumed that f=f⁡(x,t)f=f(x,t) and f~=f~​(t)\tilde{f}=\tilde{f}(t) are nonnegative functions satisfying the following properties

f∈L∞​(Ω×(0,∞)),∫0∞‖f−f~‖L1​(Ω)​dt<∞,\begin{split}f\in L^{\infty}\big(\Omega\times(0,\infty)\big),\\ \\ \int_{0}^{\infty}||f-\tilde{f}||_{L^{1}(\Omega)}\hskip 2.84544ptdt<\infty,\end{split} (10)

which are also considered in (5) for system (4). However, for our proof, we need to also assume a stronger convergence of ff to f~\tilde{f} in the sense that

∫0∞‖f−f~‖L2​(Ω)2​𝑑t+∫0∞‖∫Ωf−f~‖L2​(Ω)2​𝑑t<∞.\int_{0}^{\infty}||f-\tilde{f}||^{2}_{L^{2}(\Omega)}\hskip 2.84544ptdt+\int_{0}^{\infty}\Big|\Big|\int_{\Omega}f-\tilde{f}\Big|\Big|^{2}_{L^{2}(\Omega)}\hskip 2.84544ptdt<\infty. (11)

In contrast, the second hypothesis for ff in (5) regarding the integrability in time of ‖∇f‖L2​(Ω)2||\nabla f||_{L^{2}(\Omega)}^{2} is not needed for our study.

In the most natural case in which f~\tilde{f} is periodic, ff represents a source term that is asymptotically periodic in time, globally bounded, and whose spatial heterogeneities decay in time, in the sense that the second part of (10) and (11) hold. This models a persistent global periodic source with certain localized spatial perturbations that are however controlled in the long term.

For instance, ff can be taken as

f⁡(x,t)=f~​(t)+p⁡(t)​q​(x),f(x,t)=\tilde{f}(t)+p(t)q(x),

where f~∈L∞​((0,∞))\tilde{f}\in L^{\infty}\big((0,\infty)\big) is time periodic, q∈L1​(Ω)∩L∞​(Ω)q\in L^{1}(\Omega)\cap L^{\infty}(\Omega) encapsulates the spatial heterogeneities, and p∈L1​((0,∞))∩L∞​((0,∞))p\in L^{1}\big((0,\infty)\big)\cap L^{\infty}\big((0,\infty)\big) represents the time decay of such heterogeneities.

In nature, there are various examples of chemotactic processes exhibiting such periodic dynamics. For instance, in the presence of the chemoattractant cyclic AMP, in [18] the movement of Dictyostelium discoideum amoebae was analyzed, concluding that the average velocity towards their center of aggregation is periodic in time. An example more closely related to our scenario was reported in [25], in which E. coli cells were exposed to spatially and temporally varying attractant sources. It was shown that at low source frequencies, the bacterial population density oscillates in synchrony with the periodically supplied attractant.

These observations provide a biological motivation for analyzing the long-time behavior of Keller-Segel-type systems subject to periodic external inputs, and for identifying the conditions under which the macroscopic variables inherit the periodicity of the source.

The article is structured as follows. After this introduction, Section 2 covers the global existence of bounded solutions to the system, while Section 3 includes further estimates that allow us to prove that the solution uu converges to u¯​(t):=1|Ω|​∫Ωu⁡(x,t)​𝑑x\displaystyle\bar{u}(t)\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\frac{1}{|\Omega|}\int_{\Omega}u(x,t)\hskip 2.84544ptdx. The main result of the article, Theorem 4.1 is included in Section 4, proving that indeed u¯​(t)\bar{u}(t) converges to u~​(t)\tilde{u}(t), and proceeding similarly for vv. A final discussion concerning the case in which f~\tilde{f} is time periodic is included in Section 5, with some comments regarding the conditions under which the solutions to the ODE system (8) inherit the periodicity of f~\tilde{f}.

2 Existence and uniqueness of solutions

In this section we present Theorem 2.1, the main result concerning the global existence of bounded solutions to system (1). For brevity reasons, as the proof is similar to others and mainly follows the steps in [22], we only provide an outline of it.

Theorem 2.1.

Let Ω⊂ℝn\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}, n≥1n\geq 1 be a convex, bounded domain with smooth boundary and assume that f∈L∞​(Ω×(0,∞))f\in L^{\infty}\big(\Omega\times(0,\infty)\big), u0∈C0​(Ω¯)u_{0}\in C^{0}(\bar{\Omega}) and v0∈W1,∞​(Ω)v_{0}\in W^{1,\infty}(\Omega). Then, for all χ∈ℝ\chi\in\mathbb{R}, D>0D>0 and a≥0a\geq 0 there exists r0>0r_{0}>0 such that if r≥r0r\geq r_{0}, problem (1) with boundary and initial conditions (2) admits a uniquely determined nonnegative global classical solution (u,v)(u,v) with

‖u‖L∞​(Ω)+‖v‖W1,∞​(Ω)<c,for all ​t>0,||u||_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}+||v||_{W^{1,\infty}(\Omega)}<c,\quad\text{for all }t>0,

for a certain c>0c>0 independent of tt.

Sketch of the proof As above mentioned, the proof can be carried out similarly as in [22]. Firstly, the local existence of solutions in an interval (0,Tmax)(0,T_{\max}) is standard following the results by Amann [1]. Then, after appropriate estimates for the quantity ∑k=0mbk​∫Ωuk​|∇v|2​m−2​k\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{m}b_{k}\int_{\Omega}u^{k}|\nabla v|^{2m-2k}, for conveniently selected weights bkb_{k}, time-independent bounds for uu in Lm​(Ω)L^{m}(\Omega) and for ∇v\nabla v in L2​m​(Ω)L^{2m}(\Omega) can be obtained for arbitrarily large m∈ℕm\in\mathbb{N}. The main difference with respect to [22] lies on the conditions for r0r_{0} based on previois estimates that depend on ‖f‖L∞​(Ω×(0,∞))||f||_{L^{\infty}(\Omega\times(0,\infty))}. Lastly, standard semigroup theory allows to obtain the desired bounds for uu and vv.

3 Further estimates

Next, we derive some estimates that play a crucial role when analyzing the asymptotic behavior of the solutions. The first result entails a lower bound for the total mass of uu.

Lemma 3.1.

Let ff be such that ‖f‖L∞​(Ω×(0,∞))<∞||f||_{L^{\infty}(\Omega\times(0,\infty))}<\infty. Then, if r>0r>0 is large enough, there exists c>0c>0 satisfying

∫Ωu≥c,for all ​t>0.\int_{\Omega}u\geq c,\quad\text{for all }t>0.
Proof.

Firstly, the assumptions on ff and rr ensure that by Theorem 2.1 there exists a unique global solution (u,v)(u,v) to system (1), satisfying u∈L∞​(Ω×(0,∞))u\in L^{\infty}\big(\Omega\times(0,\infty)\big) and v∈L∞​((0,∞),W1,∞​(Ω))v\in L^{\infty}\big((0,\infty);\penalty\ W^{1,\infty}(\Omega)\big).

The main part of the proof follows the method introduced by Mizukami and Yokota in [13], Lemma 4.2. To this end, we take an arbitrary β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1) satisfying

0<β<min⁡{1,4​(r−‖v‖L∞​(Ω×(0,∞)))D​χ2​‖∇v‖L∞​(Ω×(0,∞))2−1},0<\beta<\min\left\{1,\frac{4\left(r-||v||_{L^{\infty}\left(\Omega\times(0,\infty)\right)}\right)}{D\chi^{2}||\nabla v||^{2}_{L^{\infty}(\Omega\times(0,\infty))}}-1\right\}, (12)

and consider ∫Ωu−β\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}u^{-\beta}. In particular, the choice of r>0r>0 must be large enough to satisfy

r>D⋅χ2⋅‖∇v‖L∞​(Ω×(0,∞))24+‖v‖L∞​(Ω×(0,∞)),r>\frac{D\cdot\chi^{2}\cdot||\nabla v||^{2}_{L^{\infty}\left(\Omega\times(0,\infty)\right)}}{4}+||v||_{L^{\infty}\left(\Omega\times(0,\infty)\right)}, (13)

ensuring that indeed β>0\beta>0. Integrating by parts we obtain

dd​t​∫Ωu−β=−β∫Ωu−β−1(DΔu−χ∇⋅(u∇v)+ru(1−u−vr))=−Dβ(β+1)∫Ωu−β−2|∇u|2−χβ(β+1)∫Ωu−β−1∇u⋅∇v−rβ∫Ωu−β(1−u−vr), for all t>0.\begin{split}\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega}u^{-\beta}=&-\beta\int_{\Omega}u^{-\beta-1}\Bigg(D\Delta u-\chi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v)+ru\left(1-u-\frac{v}{r}\right)\Bigg)\\ =&-D\beta(\beta+1)\int_{\Omega}u^{-\beta-2}|\nabla u|^{2}-\chi\beta(\beta+1)\int_{\Omega}u^{-\beta-1}\nabla u\cdot\nabla v\\ &-r\beta\int_{\Omega}u^{-\beta}\left(1-u-\frac{v}{r}\right),\quad\text{ for all t>0}.\end{split} (14)

The term involving the product of the gradients can be bounded using Young’s inequality as follows

−χβ(β+1)∫Ωu−β−1∇u⋅∇v≤χβ(β+1)∫Ωu−β−1|∇u||∇v|≤D​β​(β+1)​∫Ωu−β−2​|∇u|2+D​β​(β+1)​χ24​∫Ωu−β​|∇v|2,\begin{split}-\chi\beta(\beta+1)\int_{\Omega}u^{-\beta-1}\nabla u\cdot\nabla v\leq\chi\beta(\beta+1)\int_{\Omega}u^{-\beta-1}|\nabla u||\nabla v|\\ \leq D\beta(\beta+1)\int_{\Omega}u^{-\beta-2}|\nabla u|^{2}+\frac{D\beta(\beta+1)\chi^{2}}{4}\int_{\Omega}u^{-\beta}|\nabla v|^{2},\end{split} (15)

for all t>0t>0. Notice that the first term appearing on the right hand side here cancels the corresponding one in (14). We can moreover estimate the final term in (15) by making use of the L∞​(Ω×(0,∞))L^{\infty}\big(\Omega\times(0,\infty)\big) bound for ∇v\nabla v. In particular, for all t>0t>0 we have

D​β​(β+1)​χ24∫Ωu−β|∇v|2≤||∇v||2L∞​(Ω×(0,∞)CLOSE⋅D​β​(β+1)​χ24∫Ωu−β.\frac{D\beta(\beta+1)\chi^{2}}{4}\int_{\Omega}u^{-\beta}|\nabla v|^{2}\leq||\nabla v||^{2}_{L^{\infty}(\Omega\times(0,\infty)}\cdot\frac{D\beta(\beta+1)\chi^{2}}{4}\int_{\Omega}u^{-\beta}. (16)

Next, concerning the last term appearing in (14), we have

Next, we prove a similar result concerning a lower bound for the solution u~\tilde{u} to the associated ODE system. In this case it is again a threshold for the logistic growth rate rr which drives the dynamics of the system.

With respect to F1F_{1}, by means of an integration by parts followed by Young’s inequality, we have

Next, we prove another integrability property, this time for ∫Ω(|Δ​v|2+|∇v|2)\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}\Big(|\Delta v|^{2}+|\nabla v|^{2}\Big).

Lemma 3.4.

Let ff be such that hypotheses (10) and (11) hold for a certain f~\tilde{f}. Then, if r>0r>0 is large enough in the sense of the previous lemmas, there exists c>0c>0 such that

∫0∞∫Ω(|Δ​v|2+|∇v|2)​𝑑x​𝑑t≤c<∞.\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{\Omega}\Big(|\Delta v|^{2}+|\nabla v|^{2}\Big)dx\hskip 2.84544ptdt\leq c<\infty.
Proof.

We begin by noting that the second equation in (1) can be rewritten as

∂v∂t−Δ​v+v−f+∫Ωf−∫Ωv=a​u−a​∫Ωu+∫Ω∂v∂t,\frac{\partial v}{\partial t}-\Delta v+v-f+\int_{\Omega}f-\int_{\Omega}v=au-a\int_{\Omega}u+\int_{\Omega}\frac{\partial v}{\partial t}, (49)

for all t>0t>0, due to having

∫Ω∂v∂t=a​∫Ωu−∫Ωv+∫Ωf,\int_{\Omega}\frac{\partial v}{\partial t}=a\int_{\Omega}u-\int_{\Omega}v+\int_{\Omega}f,

as a result of directly integrating the equation over Ω\Omega. Thus, multiplying equation (49) by −Δ​v-\Delta v and integrating over Ω\Omega, we obtain

−∫Ω[(∂v∂t−∫Ω∂v∂t)​Δ​v]+∫Ω|Δ​v|2−∫Ω[(v−∫Ωv)​Δ​v]=−∫Ω[(f−∫Ωf)Δv]−a∫Ω[(u−∫Ωu)Δv],for all t>0.\begin{split}-\int_{\Omega}&\left[\left(\frac{\partial v}{\partial t}-\int_{\Omega}\frac{\partial v}{\partial t}\right)\Delta v\right]+\int_{\Omega}|\Delta v|^{2}-\int_{\Omega}\left[\left(v-\int_{\Omega}v\right)\Delta v\right]\\ &=-\int_{\Omega}\left[\left(f-\int_{\Omega}f\right)\Delta v\right]-a\int_{\Omega}\left[\left(u-\int_{\Omega}u\right)\Delta v\right],\quad\text{for all }t>0.\end{split} (50)

Next, we consider the following identities that hold for all t>0t>0

−∫Ω[(∂v∂t−∫Ω∂v∂t)Δv]=12​dd​t​∫Ω|∇v|2,−∫Ω[(v−∫Ωv)Δv]=∫Ω|∇v|2,−a∫Ω[(u−∫Ωu)Δv]≤14​∫Ω|Δ​v|2+a2​∫Ω(u−∫Ωu)2,−∫Ω[(f−∫Ωf)Δv]≤14​∫Ω|Δ​v|2+∫Ω(f−∫Ωf)2.\begin{split}-\int_{\Omega}\left[\left(\frac{\partial v}{\partial t}-\int_{\Omega}\frac{\partial v}{\partial t}\right)\Delta v\right]&=\frac{1}{2}\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega}|\nabla v|^{2},\\ \\ -\int_{\Omega}\left[\left(v-\int_{\Omega}v\right)\Delta v\right]&=\int_{\Omega}|\nabla v|^{2},\\ \\ -a\int_{\Omega}\left[\left(u-\int_{\Omega}u\right)\Delta v\right]&\leq\frac{1}{4}\int_{\Omega}|\Delta v|^{2}+a^{2}\int_{\Omega}\left(u-\int_{\Omega}u\right)^{2},\\ \\ -\int_{\Omega}\left[\left(f-\int_{\Omega}f\right)\Delta v\right]&\leq\frac{1}{4}\int_{\Omega}|\Delta v|^{2}+\int_{\Omega}\left(f-\int_{\Omega}f\right)^{2}.\end{split} (51)

The first two are a direct consequence of having ∫ΩΔ​v=0\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}\Delta v=0 due to the Neumann homogeneous boundary conditions and a standard integration by parts, while the third and fourth one follow directly from the pointwise identity −A​B≤14​A2+B2\displaystyle-AB\leq\frac{1}{4}A^{2}+B^{2} for any A,B∈ℝA,B\in\mathbb{R}.

In this way, (50) can be expressed as

12​dd​t∫Ω|∇v|2+∫Ω|Δ​v|2+∫Ω|∇v|2≤12​∫Ω|Δ​v|2+a2​∫Ω(u−∫Ωu)2+∫Ω(f−∫Ωf)2,\begin{split}\frac{1}{2}\frac{d}{dt}&\int_{\Omega}|\nabla v|^{2}+\int_{\Omega}|\Delta v|^{2}+\int_{\Omega}|\nabla v|^{2}\\ &\leq\frac{1}{2}\int_{\Omega}|\Delta v|^{2}+a^{2}\int_{\Omega}\left(u-\int_{\Omega}u\right)^{2}+\int_{\Omega}\left(f-\int_{\Omega}f\right)^{2},\end{split} (52)

for all t>0t>0. Considering that ∫Ω(u−∫Ωu​𝑑x)2​𝑑x\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}\left(u-\int_{\Omega}u\hskip 2.84544ptdx\right)^{2}dx is precisely the function k1k_{1} defined in (26), whose integrability was proven in Lemma 3.3, and the fact that ∫0∞∫Ω(f−∫Ωf​𝑑x)2​𝑑x​𝑑t<∞\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{\Omega}\left(f-\int_{\Omega}f\hskip 2.84544ptdx\right)^{2}dx\hskip 2.84544ptdt<\infty due to (11), as seen in Lemma 3.3, integrating (52) in time over (0,∞)(0,\infty) yields the desired result. ∎

Lemma 3.5.

Lemma 3.7.

4 Asymptotic behavior: convergence to the associated ODE system

The main result in this work concerns the asymptotic behavior of the solutions to the original system (1). In particular, the convergence to the solution associated ODE system (8), as stated in the following theorem.

Theorem 4.1.

Let Ω⊂ℝn\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} be a bounded convex domain with smooth boundary and ff be a positive function satisfying (10) and (11). Then, for all χ∈ℝ\chi\in\mathbb{R}, D>0D>0 and a≥0a\geq 0 there exists r0>0r_{0}>0 such that if r≥r0r\geq r_{0}, system (1) under initial and boundary conditions (2) admits a unique solution (u,v)(u,v) such that

‖u−u~‖L2​(Ω)+‖v−v~‖L2​(Ω)→0,as ​t→∞,||u-\tilde{u}||_{L^{2}(\Omega)}+||v-\tilde{v}||_{L^{2}(\Omega)}\to 0,\quad\text{as }t\to\infty,

where (u~,v~)(\tilde{u},\tilde{v}) is the solution to the ODE system (8) with initial values (9).

The first stage of the proof is to show that, using the results from the previous section, uu, converges to u¯\bar{u}, given by

u¯​(t):=∫Ωu⁡(x,t)​𝑑x,for all ​t>0.\bar{u}(t)\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\int_{\Omega}u(x,t)\hskip 2.84544ptdx,\quad\text{for all }t>0.

Subsequently, the second part consists in proving that u¯\bar{u} indeed converges to u~\tilde{u}, the solution to the ODE system (8), and thus uu will converge to u~\tilde{u}. A similar argument will allow us to directly obtain the convergence of vv to v~\tilde{v}.

The following Lemma plays a key role in assessing the convergence.

Lemma 4.2 (Lemma 5.1 in Friedman-Tello [4]).

Let k:[0,∞)→ℝk\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R} be a C1C^{1} function satisfying

  1. 1.

    k⁡(t)≥0k(t)\geq 0 for all t>0t>0,

  2. 2.

    There exists C>0C>0 such that |k′​(t)|≤C|k^{\prime}(t)|\leq C for all t>0t>0,

  3. 3.

    ∫0∞k⁡(t)​𝑑t<∞\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}k(t)\hskip 2.84544ptdt<\infty,

then k⁡(t)→0k(t)\to 0 as t→∞t\to\infty.

With it, we finish the section with the proof of Theorem 4.1.

k1​(t):=∫Ω(u⁡(x,t)−∫Ωu⁡(x,t)​𝑑x)2​𝑑x,k_{1}(t)\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\int_{\Omega}\left(u(x,t)-\int_{\Omega}u(x,t)\penalty\ dx\right)^{2}dx,

defined in (26). Clearly, k1​(t)≥0k_{1}(t)\geq 0 for any t>0t>0, its time derivative is bounded by Lemma 3.7 and the function is integrable in time by Lemma 3.3. Thus,

k1​(t):=‖u−∫Ωu‖L2​(Ω)2→0,as ​t→∞.k_{1}(t)\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\Bigg|\Bigg|\displaystyle u-\int_{\Omega}u\Bigg|\Bigg|_{L^{2}(\Omega)}^{2}\to 0,\quad\text{as }t\to\infty.

and consider F2​(t)F_{2}(t) as given by (31), this is

5 Periodicity

Lastly, once the convergence to (u~,v~)(\tilde{u},\tilde{v}) has been established, we include some final remarks regarding its qualitative properties in the case in which f~\tilde{f} is a periodic function. The natural question that arises is whether the solution (u~,v~)(\tilde{u},\tilde{v}) does inherit the periodicity of f~\tilde{f} or not.

As mentioned in the Introduction, the ODE system (8) was considered in [5] for a=0a=0, and a periodic function f~\tilde{f} of period T>0T>0, having

{d​u~d​t=ru~(1−u~)−u~v~,t>0,d​v~d​t=−v~+f~,t>0,\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{d\tilde{u}}{dt\penalty\ }=r\tilde{u}(1-\tilde{u})-\tilde{u}\tilde{v},\quad&t>0,\\ \\ \displaystyle\frac{d\tilde{v}}{dt\penalty\ }=-\tilde{v}+\tilde{f},\quad&t>0,\end{cases} (71)

with initial values

u~​(0)=∫Ωu0​(x)​𝑑x,v~​(0)=∫Ωv0​(x)​𝑑x.\tilde{u}(0)=\int_{\Omega}u_{0}(x)\penalty\ dx,\quad\tilde{v}(0)=\int_{\Omega}v_{0}(x)\penalty\ dx.

As the second equation is uncoupled, the system can be explicitly solved, determining the threshold value

rmin:=1T​∫0Tf~​(s)​𝑑s,r_{\min}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\displaystyle\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}\tilde{f}(s)\hskip 2.84544ptds, (72)

the average value of f~\tilde{f} over its period. It is proven in the paper that if r>rminr>r_{\min}, then system (71) admits a unique positive periodic solution, that can be constructed by adequately selecting u~​(0)\tilde{u}(0) and v~​(0)\tilde{v}(0). In particular, the unique periodic solution corresponds to the pair of initial values (u~​(0),v~​(0))=(u0p​e​r,v0p​e​r)(\tilde{u}(0),\tilde{v}(0))=(u^{per}_{0},v^{per}_{0}), where

u0p​e​r​(r)=e∫0T(r−f~​(s))​𝑑s−1∫0T(r​e∫0s(r−f~​(τ))​𝑑τ)​𝑑s,v0p​e​r​(r)=1eT−1​∫0Tf~​(s)​es​ds.\begin{split}u^{per}_{0}(r)&=\frac{e^{\displaystyle\int_{0}^{T}(r-\tilde{f}(s))\penalty\ ds}-1}{\displaystyle\int_{0}^{T}\left(r\penalty\ e^{\displaystyle\int_{0}^{s}(r-\tilde{f}(\tau))\penalty\ d\tau}\right)\penalty\ ds},\\ \\ v^{per}_{0}(r)&=\frac{1}{e^{T}-1}\int_{0}^{T}\tilde{f}(s)e^{s}\penalty\ ds.\end{split} (73)


For a>0a>0, the question remains open due to the nonlinear coupling of the system. The result obtained in Lemma 3.2 provides a partial answer to this: if r>rmin,ar>r_{\min,a}, where

rmin,a:=max⁡{v~​(0),a⋅max⁡{u~​(0),1}+‖f~‖L∞​(0,∞)},r_{\min,a}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\max\big\{\tilde{v}(0),\penalty\ a\cdot\max\{\tilde{u}(0),1\}+||\tilde{f}||_{L^{\infty}(0,\infty)}\big\}, (74)

then there exists a constant c>0c>0 such that u~​(t)>c\tilde{u}(t)>c for all t>0t>0. While this rules out a decay of u~\tilde{u} to zero, it does not directly imply that (u~,v~)(\tilde{u},\tilde{v}) is TT–periodic. Moreover, rmin,ar_{\min,a} is not a sharp threshold in the sense of the decoupled case, since substituting a=0a=0 in rmin,ar_{\min,a} produces a larger value than the exact threshold rminr_{\min} obtained for a=0a=0.
